sentences.text: You're thinking of buying a new mobile phone.
Is it a need, or a want?
A need is something you can't live without.
Like rent, food and electricity.
A want makes life more enjoyable, but you can manage without it.
Ask three questions before you buy.
Can I live without it?
Without it, will my job or income suffer?
Can I wait thirty days?
If you can wait, it's most likely a want.
Wants aren't wrong.
But needs and savings come first, and wants come after that.
This video is for education only.
It is not investment advice.
I am not a SEBI-registered adviser.
Please do your own research and consult a registered adviser before you invest.
Hello!
This is the first lesson to learn before you make a budget.
The difference between needs and wants.
Many people say that by the end of the month, they don't even know where their salary went.
Most of the time, the reason is small spends on wants, disguised as needs.
Needs are the things that are essential to live, and to go to work and earn.
Rent or your home loan EMI, food, electricity, water, medical care, your children's education, and transport to work.
These are all needs.
Wants are the things that make life more enjoyable.
But we can manage without them.
Eating at restaurants, new clothes, the latest phone, several OTT subscriptions, holidays.
These are wants.
Sometimes the same item mixes a need and a want.
You could call this the grey area.
A mobile phone for work is a need.
But an expensive new model every year is a want.
You need transport to get to work.
But buying a new car when a bus or a bike would do is a want.
Food is a need.
But ordering food online every day is a want.
Before you buy something, ask yourself three questions.
The first question: can I live without it?
Second: without it, will my job or income suffer?
Third: can I wait thirty days?
Often, after thirty days, the urge is simply gone.
This is called the thirty-day rule.
Another hidden problem is lifestyle inflation.
For example, say your salary was thirty thousand.
In a few years, it rises to fifty thousand.
But if new spending on wants grows just as fast, your savings never go up.
First, for one whole month, write down every expense.
Then sort them into needs and wants.
Second, every time your salary goes up, set aside part of the raise for savings first.
Third, set a monthly limit for spending on wants.
Then enjoy spending within that limit.
In short, wants aren't wrong.
You should enjoy life too.
But the order matters.
Needs and savings first, wants after that.
In the next video, we'll use this to look at a simple budgeting rule.
